newsitem.title: CANADA: CIBC says technology forcing rules overhaul.
newsitem.headline: CIBC says technology forcing rules overhaul.

text.p: New technology is moving beyond the reach of Canada's financial regulatory system and will force an overhaul of the rules governing the country's banks, insurance companies, brokerages and trusts, the chairman of Canada's second largest bank said on Monday.
With a government task force on financial reforms expected to start next month, CIBC chairman and chief executive Al Flood said technology issues should be a top priority.
"My concern...is that new technology is moving the market beyond the reach of our regulatory system," Flood said in a speech to a Toronto business group.

"In fact, our current regulatory structures may actually inhibit the ability of Canadian companies to respond to foreign competitors right here in our home markets not to mention expanding in markets around the globe," Flood said.

Telephone and computer banking, debit cards and automated teller machines are rapidly transforming Canada's old-style bricks-and-mortar banking system. Technology has also eliminated the need for costly branch networks and lured offshore rivals to jump into Canada's consumer banking market.
Meanwhile, Canada's six major banks are spending heavily on technology to fend off so-called "virtual" banks.
The popularity of the Internet will raise difficult security issues for the banks and regulators as financial services move onto the Web, Flood said.
On the domestic front, the old lines dividing the banks, insurance, trust and securities firms have blurred, he said.
Retail stores, fund managers and insurers are demanding access to the payments system, which is currently the domain of the banks, trust companies and credit unions.
Before that occurs, however, everyone should face one group of regulators and one set of rules, Flood said, noting that the bank deals with 85 federal and provincial agencies.
"It is completely unsuited to the era we've entered -- to a financial services universe characterized by electronic and globalized commerce," Flood said.
He later told reporters that Canada's financial services sector could make due with half-a-dozen regulators if country-wide standards were adopted.
The federal government is expected to announce the membership and mandate of the task force in November. The group is scheduled to report its findings within 18 months.
